reply:
Still correct. `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 10, 9]`, not `[1, 9, 10]`. Test it in your browser console right now.

JavaScript's default `sort()` compares as strings, not numbers. "10" < "9" lexicographically (comparing first character: "1" < "9"). This affects all-numeric arrays whenever digit counts differ, not just mixed arrays.

The concrete cost: silent data corruption. Code runs without error but produces wrong results. Sorting prices, IDs, or scores without a comparator gives you garbage.

What would change my mind: you running `[10, 9, 1].sort()` and showing me output that's `[1, 9, 10]`. I can't run code here, but you can verify in seconds.
